intro: Singapore gazettes its Heritage Trees by law: a girth over five metres and a story worth keeping gets a tree lightning protection, an English information panel and legal protection from felling. Ten of them are here. Five stand within a few hundred metres of each other on Fort Canning, the hill that held the island's first prison and its first botanical experiments, which makes that the walk. The rest are scattered: a bodhi tree on Pearl's Hill, a banyan in Tiong Bahru that reached a 22.8 metre girth in under sixty years, and one reachable only by boat.
meta_description: Singapore's heritage trees, from the Tembusu on the $5 note to Fort Canning's colonial-era rain tree, Madras thorn and rosewood, all NParks-registered.
question_answer: Singapore's oldest documented tree is the Tembusu of the Botanic Gardens, estimated by NParks at over 200 years old, standing on Lawn E overlooking Swan Lake. It is the tree depicted on the back of the Singapore five-dollar note.
question_meta: The Tembusu on Lawn E, over 200 years old and the tree on Singapore's $5 note, is the country's oldest NParks-registered heritage tree.
question_context: Singapore's Heritage Tree Scheme, launched in 2001, is unusually precise as these registers go: every one of its 251 trees carries a measured girth, height and, where evidence allows, an age estimate, reviewed periodically by NParks arborists. Most entries carry no confirmed planting date at all, since they were already mature specimens when the scheme began surveying the island's remaining old growth. The Tembusu is the exception. NParks dates it to more than 200 years before the Botanic Gardens itself opened in 1859, based on its size and growth pattern relative to other tembusu of documented age, making it older than the Gardens that now contain it. Its fame outside botanical circles comes from a single distinctive branch, a low lateral limb curling out almost parallel to the ground, which illustrator Eng Siak Loy chose to draw on the reverse of Singapore's five-dollar note. Several of Fort Canning Park's own heritage trees are older by inference, planted during an early-1900s ornamental scheme whose planting records were never kept, but without a documented date none can currently outrank the Tembusu's sourced estimate.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Singapore?
faq.a: By documented age, the Tembusu on Lawn E of the Singapore Botanic Gardens, estimated by NParks at over 200 years old and predating the Gardens themselves. It is also the tree on the Singapore five-dollar note.

faq.q: Where are most of Singapore's heritage trees?
faq.a: Fort Canning Park and the Singapore Botanic Gardens hold the densest concentrations of publicly accessible heritage trees, though NParks' full register of 251 trees spans the whole island, including some on private land that are not open to visitors.

faq.q: Are Singapore's heritage trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes, every tree on this list stands in a free public park or car park, or is reached via a free boardwalk on Pulau Ubin. The Botanic Gardens itself has no admission charge, though its separate Orchid Garden does.

faq.q: What is Singapore's Heritage Tree Scheme?
faq.a: A National Parks Board program launched in 2001 that identifies and protects trees of exceptional size, age or historical value. Each of its 251 trees (as of the most recent count) has an individual profile with girth, height and species on NParks' public register.

trees.name: The Tembusu of Lawn E

location.address: Lawn E, Singapore Botanic Gardens, overlooking Swan Lake, Singapore

trees.story: This tree was already old when the Singapore Botanic Gardens opened around it in 1859. NParks estimates it at more than 200 years, based on growth patterns compared with other tembusu of known age, which makes it a survivor of whatever forest stood on this ground before the Gardens were laid out. Its most distinctive feature is a single low branch that grows out almost parallel to the ground before curling upward, a shape unusual enough that illustrator Eng Siak Loy chose this exact tree, and this exact limb, to draw on the reverse of Singapore's five-dollar note. It is the only tree ever to appear on a Singapore banknote. Tembusu wood is prized separately from the tree's fame: dense and highly resistant to termites, it has long been used in Malay boat-building and furniture, and the timber's hardness even became a figure of speech in Malay for a person with an unyielding heart. The tree's creamy-white flowers open in clusters and turn yellow with age, most fragrant in the late evening, when they once would have drawn Malayan flying foxes to feed on the fruit that follows. It stands in the free section of the Gardens, an easy walk from the Tanglin Gate, on open lawn rather than behind any barrier, close enough to Swan Lake that most visitors photograph the water first and only notice the tree, and the branch on their banknote, on the way back.
trees.access: Free, public section of Singapore Botanic Gardens, open 5am-12am daily
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from Botanic Gardens MRT station (Circle/Downtown Line), Tanglin Gate entrance

trees.name: The Fort Canning Rain Tree

location.address: Fort Canning Park, near Raffles Gardens and the steps to Hill Street, Singapore

trees.story: This rain tree spreads its umbrella-shaped canopy directly over a public stairway that carries walkers out of Fort Canning Park onto Hill Street, so almost everyone who takes those steps passes under it whether they notice or not. Rain trees only arrived in Singapore in 1876, imported from tropical America and planted heavily through the colonial coffee and nutmeg plantations that once covered much of the island, and this specimen's own planting date was never recorded, though its 4.93 metre girth points to a tree well over a century old. Its most reliable feature is not size but timing: every evening, roughly ninety minutes before sunset, its paired leaflets fold shut, and they do the same on overcast days, a light-sensitive reflex that gave the species both its English name and its Malay one, Pukul Lima, five o'clock. Fort Canning Hill itself was the seat of the ancient Kingdom of Singapura before it became a British fort and then a public park, so a tree standing sentinel over one of its main entrances is, in a small way, guarding ground with a longer history than the tree itself. Clusters of pink-and-white flowers appear through the year without a single dramatic peak, and the pods that follow ripen dark and fleshy, adding to the tree's already broad, low silhouette.
trees.access: Free, public park, open 24 hours
trees.transport: 5 minute walk from Fort Canning MRT station (Downtown Line), via the Hill Street steps
trees.notes: Planting date undocumented; age_min/age_max are an inference from girth and species growth rate, not a sourced figure. A different Fort Canning heritage tree, a Burmese banyan, collapsed nearby in January 2021; this is not that tree, and remains standing.

trees.name: The Fort Canning Madras Thorn
trees.age_estimate: age undocumented, girth grew from 7.4m to 8.5m since 2001

location.address: Fort Canning Park, path beside the Service Reservoir, Singapore

trees.story: NParks records this as the largest Madras thorn on Singapore's heritage register, an 8.5 metre girth today, up from 7.4 metres when it was first measured for the scheme in 2001. The species arrived in the region centuries ago with Portuguese and Spanish traders from tropical America, and by the mid-1900s it lined roadsides and housing estates across Singapore as a shade tree, until a caterpillar infestation through the 1970s got it stripped from most public planting. This one, tucked beside Fort Canning's old Service Reservoir rather than out on a street, survived that cull. Its crown is low, spreading and unusually bushy for a tree this size, shaggy with bird's nest ferns and other epiphytes that have colonized its branches over the decades, giving it a wilder look than its more manicured heritage-tree neighbours. Short, sharp thorns guard the base of each leaf, the source of both its common name and part of the Greek genus name, which references the fruit's resemblance to a monkey's earring. Those fruits split into coiled, rose-red pods each spring, exposing a sweet white pulp around glossy black seeds that draws yellow-vented bulbuls and Oriental magpie robins to disperse them, and the same pulp is eaten by people elsewhere in its native range as a sour-sweet snack or juice.
trees.access: Free, public park, open 24 hours
trees.transport: 8 minute walk from Fort Canning MRT station (Downtown Line)
trees.notes: Age genuinely undocumented; NParks' own register gives no planting date or estimate, only girth growth since 2001, so age_min/age_max are left at 0 rather than guessed. 'Largest of its kind' is NParks' own register claim about its own designated trees, not an unqualified cross-site superlative.

trees.name: The Fort Canning Tamalan
trees.age_estimate: likely 100+ years (planting era documented, exact date not)

location.address: Fort Canning Park, Fort Green, Singapore

trees.story: This tamalan is one of the last survivors of an ornamental planting scheme that once covered much of Fort Canning Hill in the early 1900s, when the old fort grounds were being turned into a colonial pleasure garden. NParks' own register notes that few of the tamalan planted here in that era still line the hill's paths, which makes this specimen, standing at Fort Green, a rare direct witness to that specific phase of the park's history rather than a later replacement. The species is native to Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam, where it can reach 20 to 30 metres, and it was brought to Singapore purely for its looks: a crown of delicate, feathery foliage carried on branches that spread wide and low, with flower buds that open lilac, shift to pink, and fade to white as they age. Its wood connects it to a more famous family. Dalbergia is the genus behind Brazilian rosewood and African blackwood, both prized and now heavily restricted timbers, and while this tree has never been harvested, its relatives explain why the genus carries the weight it does among furniture makers and luthiers. At 5.48 metres in girth and just under 15 metres tall, it is modest next to some of Fort Canning's other heritage trees, but it is one of the few left standing from a planting era the park's own records otherwise struggle to document.
trees.access: Free, public park, open 24 hours
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from Fort Canning MRT station (Downtown Line)
trees.notes: Planting date not documented; age is inferred from NParks' note that the species was 'extensively planted' at Fort Canning in the early 1900s, not from a source dating this specific tree.

trees.name: The Terap Nasi of the 14th Century Walk
trees.age_estimate: age undocumented, girth grew from 4.1m to 5.68m since 2001

location.address: Fort Canning Park, 14th Century Walk of History, near the Service Reservoir, Singapore

trees.story: This terap grows beside Fort Canning's 14th Century Walk of History, a path named for the hill's role as the seat of the ancient Kingdom of Singapura, and it carries plank buttresses at its base broad enough to make the connection to old ground feel physical rather than just historical. Its girth has grown from 4.1 metres, when NParks first endorsed it as a heritage tree in 2001, to 5.68 metres today, real if unspectacular proof of two and a half decades of recorded growth, though nothing in the register dates its planting itself. Botanist John Henry Corner, assistant director of the Botanic Gardens through the 1930s and 40s, documented Fort Canning's terap specimens in his standard reference Wayside Trees of Malaya, giving this small grove a paper trail most street trees never get. In the wild the species can reach 45 to 65 metres; Singapore's cultivated specimens stay far smaller, but the fruit does not: each one grows to roughly 18 centimetres, ripening from cream to brown and smelling notoriously strong when cut open, guarding a sweet white pulp locals have described as tasting like tangy marshmallow. The tree's tough, fibrous inner bark was historically stripped and worked into cordage, coarse cloth and basket lining across the region, a practical use that outlived the kingdom the walking path beside it is named for.
trees.access: Free, public park, open 24 hours
trees.transport: 8 minute walk from Fort Canning MRT station (Downtown Line)
trees.notes: Age genuinely undocumented; NParks gives only girth growth since 2001 endorsement, so age_min/age_max are left at 0 rather than guessed. Three other terap heritage trees stand nearby on the same walk and one more on Canning Rise; this entry is specifically HT 2001-12.

trees.name: The Kapok Tree of Seah Im Road

location.address: Seah Im Road public car park, at the base of Mount Faber, Singapore

trees.story: At 11.55 metres in girth, this is one of the largest-trunked trees on Singapore's entire heritage register, rising 34.6 metres from the edge of an ordinary public car park at the foot of Mount Faber. Kapok is deciduous, unusual for a tropical tree, dropping its leaves entirely before flowering, and its cream-coloured blooms open at night with a milky scent that draws bats to pollinate them, an entirely different visiting crowd than the tree gets by day. The seed pods that follow split to release a fine, water-resistant white fiber once used to stuff life jackets and mattresses worldwide, the reason the tree ended up as Puerto Rico's national tree despite originating, like this one's ancestors, in tropical America. What makes this particular specimen worth the detour is what stands twenty metres behind it in the undergrowth: a brick-entranced wartime bunker, its tunnel about 2.5 metres tall inside with small ventilation holes along the walls, largely forgotten until vegetation was cleared enough to rediscover it. Local historians believe it was built shortly before the Second World War, though its exact use, whether to hold prisoners of war or simply to store equipment and ammunition, has never been confirmed. The kapok tree is the only obvious marker for anyone trying to find it.
trees.access: Free, public car park
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from HarbourFront MRT station (Circle/North East Line), near the Mount Faber cable car base station
trees.notes: The bunker's wartime use (POW holding vs. storage) is stated by local historians as a belief, not a confirmed fact, and the story is phrased accordingly. Age of the tree itself is undocumented by NParks.

trees.name: The Mangrove Apples of Chek Jawa

location.address: Chek Jawa Wetlands, beside House No. 1, Pulau Ubin, Singapore

trees.story: These two mangrove apples are, according to NParks' own register, the only mangrove trees among Singapore's 251 heritage trees, standing together beside the old House No. 1 at Chek Jawa, on the far side of Pulau Ubin from the mainland. Getting there already takes effort: a bumboat from Changi Point to Ubin, then a walk or bike ride to the free boardwalk that lets visitors cross the wetland without touching the mud beneath it. The trees themselves spend part of every day partly submerged, rising and falling with the tide in a stretch of shoreline built almost entirely on salt tolerance. Around their bases, pneumatophores, root structures that poke straight up through the mud like a field of woody snorkels, let the trees pull in oxygen from air rather than the waterlogged, anoxic soil their main roots sit in. To manage the salt that soil carries, they concentrate it in their oldest leaves and simply shed them, a slow-motion filtering system with no equivalent among ordinary garden trees. Chek Jawa itself very nearly does not exist as a public reserve at all. It was slated for land reclamation in 2001 until a citizen-led biodiversity survey and public campaign got the plan shelved, meaning this pair of trees, unremarkable in age but singular in the register, sits inside a wetland Singapore almost paved over entirely.
trees.access: Free, public boardwalk (Chek Jawa Wetlands, 7am-7pm daily), reached via a paid bumboat to Pulau Ubin
trees.transport: Bumboat from Changi Point Ferry Terminal to Pulau Ubin, then a 20-25 minute walk or bike ride to the Chek Jawa boardwalk
trees.notes: Age undocumented by NParks for either tree; the pair's status as 'the only two mangrove trees in the Heritage Tree Register' is NParks' own register claim about its own designated trees. Coordinates are the midpoint of the two individually-surveyed trees (HT 2007-162 and HT 2007-163), roughly 20m apart at the same named location.

trees.name: The Bodhi Tree of Pearl's Hill

location.address: Pearl's Hill City Park, hilltop near the Service Reservoir gate, Singapore

trees.story: Singapore's first prison stood on this hill, and so did its first hospital for the poor. The Bodhi tree at the top of Pearl's Hill City Park carries 6.34 metres of girth and 16.9 metres of height on NParks' heritage register, and it grows over ground that held both, which is a fair trade. The hill takes its name from Captain James Pearl, who commanded the Indiana, the ship that brought Raffles to Singapore in 1819. He liked the view enough to buy the hill and plant it with pepper. Tan Tock Seng's hospital for destitute Chinese labourers opened on its slope in the 1840s and the colonial gaol followed, both long since buried under the reservoir and the police blocks that took their place. Ficus religiosa is the species the Buddha is traditionally said to have sat beneath, and it is sacred to Buddhists and Hindus alike. The leaves are the giveaway: heart-shaped, drawn out into a long tail that sheds monsoon rain and sets the whole crown trembling in almost no wind. This is not the Bodhi tree most people in Singapore mean. That one grows at the Jin Long Si Temple and has had its own long public fight over the land around it. This is a different individual on a different hill, and it draws no crowd at all. NParks records no planting date, so its age is unknown.
trees.access: Free, public park (Pearl's Hill City Park), no gates or opening hours found
trees.transport: Short walk (roughly 5-10 minutes, uphill) from Outram Park MRT station (East-West/North-East/Thomson-East Coast lines)
trees.verify_notes: Corrected 2026-08-22: the story said Captain Pearl planted the hill with nutmeg, and two sources (NParks' heritage tree record and Wikipedia's Pearl's Hill article) say pepper; the gambier belongs to the occupants before him.

trees.name: The Banyan of Tiong Bahru Park
trees.age_estimate: under 60 years (planted after the park opened in 1967)

location.address: Tiong Bahru Park, Singapore

trees.story: A girth of 22.8 metres usually takes a tree several centuries. This one managed it in under sixty years. Tiong Bahru Park was developed in 1967 and NParks' own register states plainly that the banyan was planted after that, which makes it younger than the flats around it and still one of the widest trees on Singapore's heritage list. The trick is in how a banyan is put together. Ficus benghalensis drops aerial roots from its branches; they reach the ground, thicken into trunks of their own, then fuse with each other and with the original stem into a single braided mass that a tape measure reads as one enormous trunk. A banyan does not so much grow fat as recruit. Measured at the standard 1.3 metres above the ground, those 22.8 metres are really a committee. So the thing to go and look at here is not age. It is speed, and the odd architecture that produces it: a tree 18.4 metres tall occupying its patch of park like something with four times its lifespan behind it, props still coming down through the canopy in various stages of becoming trunks. In Hindu tradition the species carries its own weight, the roots read as Brahma's, the trunk as Vishnu's, the branches as Shankar's. Older banyans elsewhere in the Tiong Bahru area have been called a hundred years and more. This one, by its own record, is not among them.
trees.access: Free, public park, no gates or opening hours found
trees.transport: Roughly 10-15 minute walk from Tiong Bahru or Redhill MRT station

trees.name: The Earpod Tree of Fort Canning

location.address: Fort Canning Park, between the Fort Wall and Hotel Fort Canning, Singapore

trees.story: The seed pods explain the name: dark, flat, coiled into a near-perfect circle and close enough to a human ear that the tree is called after one in both Spanish and English. In Costa Rica, where the same species is the national tree, those pods are a roadside fixture. The earpod at Fort Canning has been on Singapore's heritage register since 2001, with 5.94 metres of girth and 17.9 metres of height, standing on the path behind the Fort Wall. It came from the tropical dry forests running from Mexico down to Venezuela, where it is one of the largest trees of that habitat, reaching 40 metres with a trunk three metres through, and where old specimens push surface roots out far enough to lift nearby paving. It arrived here as an ornamental and is now the first stop on NParks' own walking trail of the hill's heritage trees, which puts four more within a few hundred metres of it. One thing is unresolved and worth knowing before you go. Both the register and NParks' current Fort Canning trail guide describe this tree standing. A 2025 travel account describes an earpod tree somewhere in the same park that came down in a 2014 storm and kept growing on its side, its trunk now carrying orchids and ferns. Nobody has confirmed whether that is this tree or another one. If you find it lying down, it is alive, and it is still worth the walk.
trees.access: Free, public park, open 24 hours
trees.transport: 8-10 minute walk from Fort Canning MRT station (Downtown Line)

trees.name: The Sausage Tree of the Sundial Garden

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, near Sundial Garden

trees.story: A ripe fruit on this tree is a grey-brown cylinder up to a metre long, hanging from a cord of a stalk, heavy enough that nobody sensible stands under one for long. That is the whole species in one glance, and it is where the name comes from. The Gardens kept the paperwork for this particular tree. It arrived from Honolulu on 13 May 1931 and went into the ground on 19 October the same year, one of the tropical species being trialled here for economic and medicinal value, in an era when whether a plant was useful decided whether it earned a place. It has held its patch of lawn beside the Sundial Garden ever since. In its native Africa the fruit is both useful and dangerous. Raw it is poisonous. Processed it goes into herbal remedies and fermented drinks, and in several communities a fruit is buried in place of a body when there is no body to bury. The flowers that come before it are deep maroon, smell of nothing anyone would choose, and open at night for bats rather than bees. Ninety-five years in, though, the sausages are the point. Once set they hang for months, which makes this one of the few trees on this list with something to show whichever week you turn up.
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 10 minute walk

trees.name: The Baobab of Melati Gate

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, near Melati Gate, Cluny Park Road

trees.story: There is a baobab in Singapore, and it is only about forty years old. Everything worth knowing about it follows from those two facts. The species belongs to dry African savannah, where it survives months without rain by storing water in a swollen trunk; Singapore delivers rain most weeks and grows very few baobabs from seed. This is thought to be one of the handful that were. NParks put it at close to thirty years old when it was endorsed as a heritage tree in 2016, which makes it around forty now. For a species that can pass a thousand years, that is a child, and it already carries five metres of girth. Baobab trunks swell out of all proportion to their height as they age, so a young one looks like a fat grey bottle with twigs on top. This is exactly that. It has moved once. In June 1996 it was lifted from elsewhere in the Gardens and replanted here beside Melati Gate on the Cluny Park Road side, a long way from the busier lawns, which is why most visitors never meet it. Its flowers are worth knowing about even if you will not see them: large, white, hanging upside down, opening after dark for bats to pollinate, and finished inside a day.
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 15-20 minute walk to the Bukit Timah Core / Cluny Park Road side

trees.name: The Cannon Ball Tree of the Ginger Garden

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, Ginger Garden, behind the waterfall

trees.story: This tree flowers and fruits straight out of its own trunk. Ropes of waxy pink and cream flowers erupt from the bark, and behind them hang the fruit it is named for, brown spheres the size of cannon balls that crack open on the ground and smell appalling for days afterwards. It grew from seed collected in a hurry. In 1931 E.J.H. Corner, then an assistant director of the Botanic Gardens, was sailing back from home leave in England when his ship called at Colombo. He had eight hours before it left again, spent them getting up to the botanic garden at Peradeniya near Kandy, and came back aboard with cannon ball seed. This tree was planted from it that year, behind the waterfall at the edge of the Ginger Garden. The flowers make no nectar, and the pollen in the ring at their centre is sterile. Carpenter bees come for that sterile pollen anyway and collect the fertile kind on their backs on the way in, which is the arrangement the entire species runs on. Two degrees off the equator there is no season to wait for; it flowers and fruits more or less continuously. Half a dozen more heritage trees stand within about five hundred metres, which makes this the one stretch of this list you can walk rather than travel between.
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 10-15 minute walk to the Ginger Garden

trees.name: The Nutmegs of the Economic Garden

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, Central Core, near the former Economic Garden site

trees.story: Orchard Road is named after orchards, and the crop in them was nutmeg. Singapore grew it hard through the 1840s until disease went through the plantations in the 1860s and took the industry with it. These two trees are not survivors of that boom. They are the closest thing to it still growing in the city. They stand a few metres apart in the Central Core, on the ground of the Gardens' Economic Garden, laid out in 1879 to work out which tropical crops could be made to pay here. Nutmeg was already the answer that had failed, kept on as a specimen, and this pair are among the last of those crop plants left standing. The register lists them separately. A visitor sees one thing: two trunks a little over a metre round each, neither the sort of bulk that stops anyone in their tracks. What they do have is fruit. Nutmeg trees are either male or female, and both of these are female. The fruit is a yellow, apricot-shaped thing that splits to show a scarlet lace cage wrapped around a single dark seed. The cage is mace. The seed is nutmeg. One tree, two spices, priced separately for centuries. Nobody recorded when either of them went in. If you know, tell us.
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 15-20 minute walk to the Central Core

trees.name: The Burmese Banyan of Swan Lake

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, between Swan Lake and Marsh Garden

trees.story: Fifteen metres of girth, and almost none of it is a trunk in the ordinary sense. This is a strangler fig, and what a tape measure reads at chest height is a fused colonnade of pillar roots dropped from the branches over a century and more, thickened where they hit the ground and grown together since. It carries that mass 22 metres up, on the edge of Swan Lake. NParks will not date it. The register says only that it is thought to be as old as the Gardens themselves, which opened in 1859, and that is a tradition rather than a record. What is firmer than the tradition: the tree turns up in old paintings of the Gardens, and Herbarium staff have recalled playing around it as children in the 1930s, so it was already a landmark before the war. Even its name is unsettled. It is registered as Ficus kurzii, the Burmese banyan, but a fig specialist writing in 2024 points out that true wild kurzii does not grow this far south down the Malay Peninsula, and argues this tree is more likely a hybrid with Ficus benjamina, propagated here from cuttings for more than 150 years. So: one of the largest things growing in the Gardens, and still an open question as to what it actually is.
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 10 minute walk to Swan Lake

trees.name: The Saga Tree of the Tanglin Entrance

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, near Frangipani Garden / the Lady on a Hammock sculpture, close to the Tanglin Entrance

trees.story: The saga was brought to Singapore to fight a grass. Between 1883 and 1885 the Gardens' superintendent Nathaniel Cantley planted it as an experiment in smothering lalang, the coarse weed grass that takes any cleared ground here within weeks. It worked well enough that the director Henry Ridley later used saga to shade the Gardens' nutmeg, and by the 1970s and 80s it had become a standard Singapore roadside tree. This one grows a few minutes inside the Tanglin entrance, near the Frangipani Garden. Its age comes out of a filing cabinet rather than off a tape. The earliest herbarium specimen cut from this individual tree is dated 1900, which is why the register says it must be well over a century old, putting it past 126 years now. Its measurements are less settled. NParks records a girth of 5.32 metres and a height of 13.1 metres; the National Heritage Board's own entry gives 4.8 metres and 24 metres. The height gap is far too wide to split, so treat both as claims and neither as final. What nobody disputes is the seeds, hard scarlet discs that children pocket and collectors hunt; one collector has mapped 57 saga trees across the island. This tree also sits in a national art collection, photographed by Robert Zhao Renhui for his 2013 work mapping exactly those trees.
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 5-10 minute walk from the Tanglin Gate

trees.name: The Jelutong of Lawn S

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, Lawn S, near Lower Ring Road within the rainforest

trees.story: You can see this tree from the Bandstand, which is odd for a tree standing inside a forest. The jelutong is an emergent: it does not stop at the canopy but pushes its crown out above it, and at 29 metres this one clears everything around it. What is around it matters as much as the tree. It grows on Lawn S, inside the Gardens' patch of primary rainforest, one of only two fragments of Singapore's original forest left anywhere on the island. The species is native here, so this is a tree standing in something close to the vegetation it evolved in, in the middle of a city that has built over almost all of it. Its sap made chewing gum. Gutta jelutong was tapped across Malaya as a base for the stuff, and the pale, soft timber went into pencils, which is a strange double career for a tree in a country that banned the sale of chewing gum in 1992. Nobody has dated it. The register offers no estimate at all, only four metres of girth and that height, and for once the height is the more interesting number: a native tree, in native forest, tall enough to be picked out from a lawn several hundred metres away. If anyone has measured or dated this one, we would like to hear it.
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 15 minute walk to the rainforest section

trees.name: The Mandela Tree of Orchid Plaza

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, Orchid Plaza

trees.story: When Nelson Mandela came to the Singapore Botanic Gardens in 1997, the Gardens dedicated a tree to him, and they picked an unlikely one. The giant cola is West African, unlike anything else growing around Orchid Plaza, and it has stood there with his name attached ever since. An orchid was named for the same visit, which is the more Singaporean gesture. The tree is the one you can walk up to. Cola gigantea belongs to the genus behind the original cola drinks. Its nuts are bitter and loaded with caffeine, chewed across West Africa as a stimulant and offered to guests as a matter of courtesy, and almost every part of the tree has a use in traditional medicine: bark for swellings and pain, other parts against fever, asthma and whooping cough. Laboratory work on its leaf extracts has since taken an interest in the anti-inflammatory half of that reputation. It is not a giant here. Three and a half metres of girth and fifteen metres of height is respectable rather than startling, and it only joined the heritage register in 2014, seventeen years after the dedication. Nobody recorded when it was planted. A dedication is not a planting, so its age is genuinely unknown, and no record of one has turned up.
trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 15-20 minute walk to Orchid Plaza near the National Orchid Garden

trees.name: The African Butter Tree of the Healing Garden

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, Healing Garden (behind Block 5)

trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 15-20 minute walk to the Healing Garden
trees.story:
The seeds of this tree are roughly forty percent fat, and West Africa presses them for butter. That is what brought it to Singapore. In 1897 the Botanic Gardens had it sent from Sierra Leone and planted in the Economic Garden, the plot where the colony tested which tropical crops could be made to pay. Pentadesma butyracea grows wild from Guinea to Cameroon and nowhere in Southeast Asia. The oil never became a business here, and the experiment settled into being a specimen instead.

NParks calls this tree likely a remnant of that original introduction and says it has stood on this spot for more than a century. That word likely is why its age sits as a band, roughly 110 to 140 years, rather than a date. The measurements are firmer: 3.2 metres round in 2003, 3.6 metres now, and 18 metres of crown over the Healing Garden.

A survey of Southeast Asian plant resources records the species growing successfully in Singapore by about 1900, which confirms the experiment took even though the trade never did.

The fruit is the size of a fist, ten to twelve centimetres, with a rind that takes a knife and a yellow greasy juice inside. The seeds within are the part anyone wanted. It now stands in the Healing Garden behind Block 5, doing nothing commercial at all.

trees.name: The Teak of the Botany Centre

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, along Office Ring Road, Botany Centre

trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 10-15 minute walk to the Botany Centre
trees.story:
Teak needs a dry season, and Singapore has never had one. NParks says so on this tree's own record: the species struggles in a climate without an annual drought. This one dates from 1884 by NParks' own dating, which puts it at about 140 years, and it has spent all of them growing in conditions its species is not built for. Girth 2.9 metres, height 20.6 metres.

Tectona grandis belongs to the monsoon forests of Myanmar, Thailand, India and Indochina, where it drops its leaves through the dry months. Singapore does not supply them. The tree stands instead along Office Ring Road beside the Botany Centre, which is about as far from a monsoon forest as a teak is likely to get.

Its timber is the reason anyone knows the word. Teak is loaded with natural oils that see off termites and shrug off water, which is why it has decked ships for centuries and why teak furniture tends to outlive the people who buy it. Plantations across the tropics exist for that one property.

This one was never cut. It has stood since 1884 and the only thing anybody has ever taken from it is a measurement. For a species valued almost entirely by the cubic metre, that counts as an unusual career.

trees.name: The Nemesu of the Rainforest

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, Rainforest, visible from Lower Ring Road (near the Heritage Mengkulang)

trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee. The tree itself stands inside the six-hectare rainforest patch and is not approached directly, but NParks' own page says it 'can be viewed from a nearby footpath' and it is 'easily viewed from Lower Ring Road'.
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 15 minute walk to the rainforest section
trees.story:
Forty-four and a half metres is roughly a fourteen-storey building, and that is the height of this tree, standing in the middle of Singapore. The nemesu is an emergent dipterocarp, built to push a straight bole clear of everything around it, and the species can carry that trunk to sixty metres. This one is six metres round at chest height, thick even by the standards of the city's heritage register.

It is also an endangered species, and this tree did not arrive in a pot. It stands inside the six hectares of surviving rainforest held within the Singapore Botanic Gardens, ground the Gardens grew around rather than laid out. UNESCO listed the Gardens as a World Heritage Site in 2015.

You do not walk up to it. NParks says it can be seen from a nearby footpath and is easily viewed from Lower Ring Road. The rainforest patch is not somewhere to wander into, and the tree is big enough that this hardly matters. Look for scaly bark and the plank buttresses spreading from its base.

The species has a road named after it across town, Nemesu Avenue by Lower Peirce Reservoir. Nobody has published this tree's age, and dipterocarp growth varies too much from site to site to work one out from the girth. If anyone has a figure, we would like it.

trees.name: The Mengkulang of the Gardens' Jungle

location.address: Singapore Botanic Gardens, along Lower Ring Road, near the Bandstand

trees.access: Free, Singapore Botanic Gardens is open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Botanic Gardens MRT (Circle/Downtown lines), about 15 minute walk to the rainforest section near the Bandstand
trees.story:
In 1908 Henry Ridley described a species new to science, and the material came off this tree. Heritiera elata is pinned to it: that is what a type specimen is, the individual the name itself refers back to. Ridley was the Botanic Gardens' first Director, and his note on these trees reads like a man who already had a favourite. There are two or three of these fine trees in the Gardens' Jungle, he wrote. The finest is a conspicuous object by the plant sheds.

The Gardens' Jungle is still there, a patch of remnant rainforest held inside the Botanic Gardens, and it has produced a run of type specimens over the years. A 2022 paper from the National University of Singapore, cataloguing the plants first described from Singapore ground, lists this species among them.

The trunk is the giveaway. Its plank buttresses fold vertically, in pleats running up from the base, a feature unique to the species. Four and a half metres round, twenty-six metres tall, standing along Lower Ring Road near the Bandstand.

Its age is genuinely unknown. NParks says it is probably older than the Gardens, which were laid out in 1859, but that is an impression rather than a measurement, and nobody has put a number on it. If you know better, tell us.
